speaker: Li Lu
text: The market exists primarily for the goal of channeling excess savings into productive use, into deserving companies, and creating this modern economy that has compound economic growth.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That is why the stock market exists in the first place.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Why do you have this speculative side?

speaker: Li Lu
text: It’s part of the human condition.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Warren always describes the stock market as a church with a casino attached to it.

speaker: Li Lu
text: The church is where the values are created, and the casino is almost part of the building permit, a necessary cost because of the human condition.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Four hundred years ago, when it was created, this was how you inspired the animal spirit, and 400 years later it is still doing that.

speaker: Li Lu
text: This is where you’re going to make a choice as students.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Do you want to be in the zero-sum game, or the value creation game?

speaker: Li Lu
text: That’s a personal choice.

speaker: Li Lu
text: As a society, you also have a choice.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You don’t want the casino side to be so out of proportion that it overwhelms the primary objective of why the market exists in the first place.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Those are choices on the individual level as well as for society.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Over 400 years, despite all this huge boom and bust, giant waste, somehow this mechanism has survived and continued to propel society as a core function.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It is pretty miraculous, to say the least.

speaker: Li Lu
text: For your students, it is important to make that distinction early on: What do you want to do personally?

speaker: Li Lu
text: As a society, we should also calibrate the proportion of each.

speaker: Li Lu
text: But they coexist as part of the human condition.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Now, onto AI and the market.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That’s a more complex question.

speaker: Li Lu
text: First of all, what is AI, or this wave of generative AI?

speaker: Li Lu
text: It is obviously a technology, a huge technological wave.

speaker: Li Lu
text: As a technology, we’ve been dealing with that for the last few hundred years, ever since the Industrial Revolution.

speaker: Li Lu
text: We have wave after wave of technological change, and the disruption and creation associated with it.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Through that process of creative destruction, we understand some aspects of it.

speaker: Li Lu
text: But somehow we feel this wave is different.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Every wave is different, but this wave is unusually different from anything we’ve experienced so far.

speaker: Li Lu
text: What makes it so different this time?

speaker: Li Lu
text: On the surface, you can see the pace of change, the scale involved, and the concentrated financial impact at the top, the nature of that concentrated financial impact at the top.

speaker: Li Lu
text: They’re all incredibly unprecedented.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Then you ask why that is the case.

speaker: Li Lu
text: The narrative is slightly different.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Most of the time, until this moment, we’ve been dealing with technological changes as a fundamental tool for human productivity.

speaker: Li Lu
text: With this technology, we introduce a different element.

speaker: Li Lu
text: We now have a spectrum of tool versus creature, and we begin to change on that spectrum of tool versus creature.

speaker: Li Lu
text: The moment it was first introduced, nearly four years ago, was the moment of the Turing test.

speaker: Li Lu
text: At that point, we could no longer tell from language whether it was a machine or a human.

speaker: Li Lu
text: From that point on, we were introduced to reasoning, and it began to gain more and more human features.

speaker: Li Lu
text: From reasoning comes coding.

speaker: Li Lu
text: With coding capability, it becomes an autonomously executing agent that functions much as a human does.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Then comes the collaboration of all the agents in complex and long-lasting tasks—call that long reasoning.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Much like human society, agents would organize, self-organize, prioritize, and execute tasks in an ever more sophisticated fashion, with their own language communication tools.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That’s where we are.

speaker: Li Lu
text: If you look at the Silicon Valley narrative, the generative AI will go to the stage of RSI, which we’re partially in – the idea that all the improvement would eventually be self-made, without a human in the loop.

speaker: Li Lu
text: From RSI we will come to AGI, then ASI, the intelligence level exceeding all humans, individually as well as together.

speaker: Li Lu
text: From there, you would say we’re creating somewhat of a semi-god or demigod, but a man-made creation.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Because that is so powerful and all-encompassing, the economic impact, by definition, has to be huge and therefore justify all the different investment costs.

speaker: Li Lu
text: When you have trillion-dollar IPOs, you’re all invited to participate in the IPO of a god or something.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That is the narrative, and that is what makes it different.

speaker: Li Lu
text: But if you step back and say – If this were indeed the case, what would become of humans?

speaker: Li Lu
text: We would live in a society lorded over by a man-made god, accessed by very few and understood by none.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Not even controlled – we can’t say that, because nobody understands it at that point.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Is there anyone in humanity who would like to live in that society?

speaker: Li Lu
text: My answer is probably a resounding no.

speaker: Li Lu
text: I don’t think anyone would want to live in that society.

speaker: Li Lu
text: There are only two outcomes, in a sense.

speaker: Li Lu
text: A) This technology is not progressing in that direction, and we can discuss what it is and why it is not; or B) If it is indeed progressing in that direction, we will all, at some point, unite together to stop it from becoming that.

speaker: Li Lu
text: In neither case are we going to have a man-made god living and lording over human society.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That is what distinguishes this generation of technology, why it is different, and the different impacts, particularly the financial market impact.

speaker: Li Lu
text: But leaving that aside, when you ask – Is this a useful technology?

speaker: Li Lu
text: The answer is also a resounding yes.

speaker: Li Lu
text: What is it, in essence?

speaker: Li Lu
text: If I were to give it a provisional definition, from observing what it does and where it came from – Generative AI is a machine that by applying brute compute with clever algorithms, using all human-generated data and its first derivative, come up and establish systematic contextual correlations among near-infinite variables of human-generated data and its first derivative.

speaker: Li Lu
text: In doing so, it establishes capabilities that include much of human reasoning and human intelligence.

speaker: Li Lu
text: At present, we know how it works and how to make it better, but we don’t quite understand why it works, much as to the extent that we don’t quite understand how human machinery works.

speaker: Li Lu
text: With that provisional definition, observing what is happening now, it equalizes a layer of the economy that is very helpful.

speaker: Li Lu
text: If you look at the economy, at the bottom we have energy and transportation.

speaker: Li Lu
text: On top of that sits manufacturing.

speaker: Li Lu
text: On top of that, we have communication and digital media.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Then we have an enormous amount of knowledge-based, technology-based services that synthesize all the knowledge we’ve accumulated and serve all the different layers of the economy.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Generative AI today, at its current stage, is great at synthesizing and equalizing all the knowledge and expertise that has accrued to that layer, helping all the other ones.

speaker: Li Lu
text: But it can’t change, for example, energy and transportation.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It doesn’t change manufacturing, which is essentially the combination of different molecules and atoms and transforming them into different combinations.

speaker: Li Lu
text: In communication and digitization, they’re already great synthesizers.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That is the realm where it is going.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It has not gone beyond humans.

speaker: Li Lu
text: By this extension, it may not rise to whatever the narrative would dictate or lead you to believe.

speaker: Li Lu
text: We’re still firmly within the human-generated data realm.

speaker: Li Lu
text: To go to the biological sense requires a whole different level.

speaker: Li Lu
text: For example, our—this may be going too far.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: Go for it.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: Knock yourself out.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Each cell contains let’s say at least fifty petabytes of files, and you need to multiply that by trillions to get us on the biological level.

speaker: Li Lu
text: We’re not anywhere close to getting to that level.

speaker: Li Lu
text: But what has been established already begins to tip this balance between tool versus creature.

speaker: Li Lu
text: One of the two arguments would persuade you to stop any further development without a human in the loop.

speaker: Li Lu
text: RSI – recursive self-improvement – without a human in the loop would be very dangerous.

speaker: Li Lu
text: They would develop goals and subgoals for their own purposes, and that would get them further from human control.

speaker: Li Lu
text: In summary, this technology is enormously helpful, transformative, and extraordinarily dangerous.

speaker: Li Lu
text: We have to, as a society and together as human beings, have a red line to firmly establish that whatever the self-learning or utilization of the tools, it cannot be without a human in the loop.

speaker: Li Lu
text: In other words, firmly establish it on the tool side rather than the creature side.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It’s also enormously disruptive, from employment to emotional dependency to risks from cyber to bio to nuclear.

speaker: Li Lu
text: In the end, what you want society to develop is a balanced pace of development that balances benefit and risk.

speaker: Li Lu
text: By the way, this technology will always have incremental costs.

speaker: Li Lu
text: This is fundamentally different from the internet or a bunch of previous technologies, where you have a one-time investment and can amortize it for a long time.

speaker: Li Lu
text: This is not the case.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You always have an incremental cost associated with it.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Cost, revenue, and profit are also very important.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Capital needs and financial discipline will always be in operation.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Also, the pace of development and the level of societal tolerance.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You have four or five different layers of considerations for pacing and development into it.

speaker: Li Lu
text: How does human society adapt to those kinds of changes?

speaker: Li Lu
text: Not always by planning.

speaker: Li Lu
text: We’re going to go through big boom and bust cycles, or even multiple ones.

speaker: Li Lu
text: That is the nature of how it is going to develop.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Those are the lines we have to think about as we approach this transformative, dangerous, disruptive, and costly technological wave.
